laudatory

LAW-duh-tor-ee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Laudatory is expressing praise.

Critics wrote laudatory reviews of the young pianist's opening performance.

Worked Example

The reviewer's laudatory write-up praised every detail of the new restaurant, right down to the napkins.

Laudatory describes writing or speech whose entire purpose is to express praise -- a laudatory review, letter, or speech.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

complimentary: Complimentary means expressing praise or approval in a light, everyday way — a kind remark, a nice comment, a few warm words. Laudatory is heavier machinery: it describes a whole piece of writing or speech whose entire purpose is praise, like a formal review or an award speech.

commendatory: Commendatory means expressing formal approval — an official stamp that something meets the standard, like a commendatory letter in an employee's file. Laudatory goes further than approving: a laudatory piece actively celebrates, praising merit rather than merely certifying it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

critical: expressing disapproval

dismissive: showing a lack of interest or respect

Where it sits · how total the praise is — favorable → laudatory → glowing

favorable vs. laudatory: A favorable review leans positive overall; a laudatory one is entirely devoted to praise.

glowing vs. laudatory: A glowing review goes further still, radiating enthusiastic admiration beyond simply being laudatory.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — laud

root — laud: praise (Latin (laudare))

suffix — -atory

suffix — -atory: tending to, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: laud ("praise") + -atory ("tending to") = tending to express praise.

Use the root in a new word: applaud

Use the root in a new word: applaud: The same root, combined with ad- ("toward"), gives us "applaud" -- literally, to clap praise toward someone.

Root Check

Word Choice

Laudatory describes the content of a piece of writing or speech, not a person's personality -- you'd never call a person themselves "laudatory."
